t: Maximum Segment Sum After Removals — Reverse Time Union-Find
o: We remove elements one at a time and after each removal report the largest sum of a contiguous run of still-present positive numbers. Brute-force rescanning after every removal costs O(n^2), which fails for n = 10^5. The classic trick: deletions are hard, insertions are easy — so process queries in reverse, 'adding' elements back and merging adjacent segments with Union-Find while tracking the global maximum segment sum. In Example 1, working backwards we re-add index 1 (sum 2), then 4 (sum 3), then 2 (sum 10), then 3 (sum 16), then 0 (still 16); recording the max *before* each re-add reproduces [14,7,2,2,0]. Constraints (n ≤ 1e5, unique removal indices) point exactly at near-linear union-find.
k: Process removals in reverse: deletion becomes insertion, which union-find handles in near-O(1).
Track segment sums as sizes in DSU; the answer before each re-add is the current global max.
Only neighbors q-1 and q+1 can merge with a newly restored index.

a.i: After each removal, scan the array once, summing maximal runs of non-removed elements and taking the maximum. Simple and correct, but quadratic.
s: After each query, scan all indices, accumulate runs of active elements, track the max run sum.
Append the max (0 if none) to the answer.
a.t: O(n^2) — one full scan per removal

a.i: Reversing time turns each removal into an insertion. When index q comes back, it forms a singleton segment and may merge with already-active segments at q-1 and q+1. DSU stores segment sums as weights; a running variable holds the maximum segment sum seen so far, which is exactly the answer for the state just before this re-add.
s: Iterate queries in reverse; record current max before restoring index q.
Mark q active, set its DSU weight to nums[q].
Union with active neighbors q-1 and q+1, accumulating sums into q's root.
Update the global max; finally reverse the collected answers.
a.t: O(n α(n)) — each index is inserted once and merged at most twice

w: Always reach for the reverse-time trick when a problem asks for answers after successive deletions. Pitfalls: record the max BEFORE re-adding the element (the query removes it first), use 64-bit sums (values up to 1e9 × 1e5), and remember the final answer is 0. Follow-ups: report the actual segment, or handle removals with negative numbers allowed.
